lead: Every processor answers two separate questions. How much work can one instruction do — is it RISC or CISC? And do instructions and data travel over the same path — von Neumann or Harvard? The first choice sets decode logic, code size and pipeline friendliness. The second sets whether an instruction fetch and a data read can share a clock cycle. Picking either badly costs speed, silicon area or pins. All four combinations ship in real chips: the 8086 is CISC with one bus, the 8051 is CISC with Harvard memory, and most ARM microcontrollers are RISC with Harvard buses.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.5 — the terms microprocessor, microcontroller and DSP mean little until you can see which instruction set and which memory layout each one uses.

sections.h3: Instruction set style: RISC and CISC

blocks.text: An instruction set is the list of operations a CPU can be told to do. Two styles dominate.

CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer) makes each instruction do a lot. Instruction length varies, from one to six bytes on the 8086. There are many addressing modes, and arithmetic can take a memory operand directly, as in ADD [2000h], AX. Control is microcoded: one instruction is broken into several small internal steps. A line of C becomes few instructions, so code stays compact — valuable when flash is small and costly. The 8086 and the 8051 are CISC.

RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) makes each instruction do one small thing. All instructions have the same length, usually 4 bytes on a 32-bit core. The load-store rule says only LOAD and STORE touch memory; arithmetic works on registers only. Many general registers, 16 or 32, keep operands on chip. Most instructions finish in one clock, so a pipeline can start a new instruction every cycle. The price is more instructions per line of C: a = b + c becomes load b, load c, add, store a. ARM, MIPS and RISC-V are RISC.

sections.h3: Memory organisation: von Neumann and Harvard

blocks.text: von Neumann. One memory holds both instructions and data, reached through one set of address, data and control lines. The CPU fetches an instruction, then reads or writes a variable: same wires, one job at a time. It is simple and cheap, one memory chip and one bus. Code and data share one address space, so a program can treat code as data — read a constant table held with the instructions, or patch its own instructions. The cost is time. While the bus fetches an instruction it cannot carry a data word, so the CPU waits. That limit is the von Neumann bottleneck. The 8086 uses this organisation.

Harvard. Program memory (flash, instructions only) and data memory (RAM, variables and stack) are separate, each with its own buses and address space. A fetch from flash and a read of a variable happen in the same clock cycle, so bandwidth doubles at the same clock. The price is more pins and wires, more silicon, and two address spaces — reading a table stored in flash needs a special instruction. Almost every microcontroller (8051, PIC, AVR) uses Harvard, and so do most DSPs, because a DSP inner loop wants one instruction fetch and two operand reads in every cycle.
Modified Harvard. One main memory, but separate instruction and data caches next to the CPU, so the core still fetches and loads in the same cycle. ARM Cortex-A application processors work this way.

The RISC/CISC question is about how an instruction is encoded and decoded. The Harvard/von Neumann question is about where instructions and data live and how many buses serve them. Nothing links the two answers. All four combinations ship:

items: CISC with Harvard: the 8051, microcoded variable-length instructions over separate program and data memory.
RISC with Harvard: ARM Cortex-M microcontrollers.
RISC with von Neumann: small RISC-V cores placed in an FPGA with one shared memory.

blocks.text: One sentence proves the independence: the 8051 is CISC with Harvard memory, so neither label can imply the other.

Read a datasheet this way. If the instructions are mostly a fixed four bytes, the core is probably RISC — though some RISC cores such as ARM Thumb-2 mix 16-bit and 32-bit encodings. If code and variables sit at different address ranges with different bus widths, the memory is Harvard. Then check what actually sets speed: clock frequency, pipeline depth, bus width and flash wait states. A 100 MHz RISC core that spends five cycles on every flash access (one transfer plus four wait states) delivers 20 million instructions per second, the same as a 20 MHz CISC core with single-cycle fetch. Design metrics decide which trade you want.

figure.caption: Program memory and data memory each have their own bus into the CPU, so an instruction fetch and a data read travel at the same time. On a single shared bus the two would have to take turns.

spec.title: Harvard memory organisation
spec.aria: Program memory on the left feeds the CPU over its own instruction bus while the CPU reads and writes data memory on the right over a separate data bus.

examples.question: A microcontroller CPU runs from a 20 MHz bus clock, and every 16-bit transfer on a bus takes exactly one bus cycle. (a) What is one bus cycle time? (b) On a von Neumann machine, how long does it take to fetch a 16-bit instruction and then read a 16-bit operand from memory? (c) How long on a Harvard machine with two independent 20 MHz buses? (d) What is the speedup, and how many such instruction-plus-operand pairs can each machine complete per second?
steps: Bus cycle time T = 1 / f = 1 / (20 × 10⁶ Hz) = 50 × 10⁻⁹ s = 50 ns.
von Neumann: the fetch and the operand read share one bus, so they run one after the other: 50 ns + 50 ns = 100 ns per pair.
von Neumann throughput = 1 / (100 ns) = 10 × 10⁶ = 10 million pairs per second.
Harvard: the fetch goes out on the instruction bus while the operand read goes out on the data bus in the same cycle, so the pair takes max(50 ns, 50 ns) = 50 ns.
Harvard throughput = 1 / (50 ns) = 20 × 10⁶ = 20 million pairs per second.
examples.answer: One bus cycle is 50 ns; the instruction-plus-operand pair takes 100 ns on von Neumann and 50 ns on Harvard, a speedup of 2×, giving 10 million and 20 million pairs per second.
examples.check:
f = 20e6                # bus clock, Hz
T = 1 / f               # one bus cycle, s
T_ns = T * 1e9
print(f"{T_ns:.1f}")
print(f"{2 * T_ns:.1f}")
print(f"{T_ns:.1f}")
print(f"{(2 * T_ns) / T_ns:.1f}")

traps: Saying RISC means Harvard and CISC means von Neumann. The 8051 is CISC with Harvard memory, and ARM Cortex-M is RISC with Harvard buses. The choices are independent.
Saying CISC is slow and RISC is fast. Clock frequency, pipeline depth, bus width and memory wait states decide speed; a RISC core waiting on slow flash loses to a simple CISC core.
Reading Harvard as 'twice the memory'. Harvard means two address spaces and two buses, not double capacity — a Harvard microcontroller usually has far less RAM than flash.
Saying modified Harvard has two main memories. It has one main memory with separate instruction and data caches close to the core.
Unit slips in bus timing: at 20 MHz one cycle is 1 ÷ (20 × 10⁶) = 50 ns, not 20 ns and not 20 µs.

quiz.q: State the load-store rule of RISC and name two RISC instruction sets.
quiz.a: Only load and store instructions access memory; all arithmetic works on registers. Any two of ARM, MIPS, RISC-V.

quiz.q: What is the von Neumann bottleneck?
quiz.a: Instructions and data share one memory and one bus, so a fetch and a data access cannot happen in the same bus cycle; the CPU waits and the shared bus caps throughput.

quiz.q: Why is a fixed instruction length easier to pipeline than a variable one?
quiz.a: With fixed length the next address is known before decoding (program counter + 4), so fetch can start every cycle. With variable length the decoder must finish before the next address is known, which stalls the fetch stage.

quiz.q: Give two costs of choosing Harvard memory organisation.
quiz.a: More pins and wires for two buses and larger silicon area; two address spaces, so data kept in program memory needs a special access instruction.

quiz.q: A CPU runs from a 40 MHz bus, one 16-bit transfer per bus cycle. Find the time for an instruction fetch plus an operand read on von Neumann and on Harvard, and the speedup.
quiz.a: T = 1 / (40 × 10⁶) = 25 ns. von Neumann: 25 + 25 = 50 ns. Harvard: 25 ns, since the two transfers overlap. Speedup = 50 ÷ 25 = 2×.

quiz.q: The 8051 is CISC with Harvard memory. What does this single fact prove about the RISC/CISC and Harvard/von Neumann choices?
quiz.a: That they are independent. RISC/CISC describes instruction encoding and decoding; Harvard/von Neumann describes memory and bus organisation. A chip can combine any pair, so neither label predicts the other.

quiz.q: A designer says 'we picked a RISC core, so our product will be faster'. Critique this in three sentences.
quiz.a: Speed also depends on clock frequency, pipeline depth, bus width and memory wait states. A RISC core fetching from slow flash with wait states can be slower than a CISC core at a higher clock. RISC mainly buys simpler decode and easier pipelining, not guaranteed speed.

beyond: Not for the exam. RISC-V is an open instruction set that any team can implement or extend, and it has pushed custom accelerators down to microcontroller-class chips. Vendors now mix the styles: ARM Thumb-2 uses both 16-bit and 32-bit encodings, and x86 cores translate complex instructions into simple internal operations before executing them. Research on near-memory and in-memory computing attacks the von Neumann bottleneck directly by moving arithmetic next to the data. Search 'RISC-V extensions', 'Thumb-2', 'modified Harvard cache' and 'von Neumann bottleneck in-memory computing' to go further.
